Pregnancy

Fetal hydrops: causes, assessment, treatment and newborn care

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Fetal hydrops, also called hydrops fetalis, is a serious pattern of abnormal fluid accumulation in a developing baby. It is a finding that can result from different conditions, rather than one disease with one treatment. Prompt fetal-medicine assessment helps identify the cause, consider available treatment and plan care for both the pregnant person and the baby. One scan or a general survival percentage cannot tell a family exactly what will happen.

What the scan finding means

Classical hydrops means abnormal fluid in at least two fetal compartments. These include the abdomen, the space around the lungs, the space around the heart and generalized swelling beneath the skin. It is not defined simply as fluid in any two organs. Excess amniotic fluid and a thickened or enlarged placenta may occur alongside hydrops, but they are not themselves two of the defining fetal compartments.

A single abnormal fetal fluid collection still matters. Current SMFM guidance describes a hydrops spectrum in which one systemic effusion can have many of the same underlying causes as multiple effusions and merit a similar diagnostic assessment. This does not mean that their prognosis or management is identical. Ask which fluid spaces are involved, whether other findings are present and what has changed since the previous scan.

Immune hydrops and maternal red-cell antibodies

Immune hydrops can develop when relevant maternal antibodies cross the placenta and cause severe fetal anaemia by damaging red blood cells or interfering with their production. The fetal heart has to work harder, and severe anaemia can lead to circulatory failure and fluid accumulation. Anti-D is one important antibody, but anti-c and anti-K can also cause serious fetal or newborn disease. A difference between the parents’ blood groups alone does not diagnose an affected pregnancy.

Anti-D immunoglobulin helps prevent eligible people from forming immune anti-D; it does not remove established antibodies, prevent every red-cell antibody or treat nonimmune hydrops. Follow the maternity team’s blood-group, antibody-testing and prevention plan. If a clinically significant antibody is already present, the team assesses whether the fetus carries the relevant antigen and what monitoring or treatment is needed. A missed injection or an antibody result is not by itself a prediction of fetal harm.

Nonimmune hydrops has many possible causes

Nonimmune hydrops means that red-cell alloimmunization is not the cause. It can occur with structural heart problems, an abnormal heart rhythm, severe anaemia from another cause, infection, chromosome or single-gene conditions, lymphatic abnormalities, lung or chest lesions, liver or metabolic disease, and some placental conditions. Examples include parvovirus infection and inherited blood disorders. Problems that affect circulation, protein balance or lymph drainage can allow fluid to accumulate.

Some complications of twins sharing a placenta can also cause hydrops and need their own specialist pathway. More than one finding may have a common genetic or other cause; identifying a heart or lung abnormality does not necessarily complete the investigation. Sometimes the cause remains uncertain even after testing. The label nonimmune does not make the condition mild, nor does uncertainty mean that assessment, monitoring or supportive care has no value.

A specialist assessment looks beyond the fluid

Ultrasound identifies the fluid pattern and assesses fetal anatomy, growth, the placenta, amniotic fluid and blood flow. A detailed fetal heart scan, or echocardiogram, examines heart structure and function. Doppler assessment of blood flow in a fetal brain artery can help assess the risk of anaemia; it does not by itself replace every confirmatory test. The team also asks about pregnancy history, family history, previous affected pregnancies, infections, relevant exposures and other medical information.

Maternal blood tests review the blood group and red-cell antibodies and may investigate infection, a blood disorder or fetal blood loss into the maternal circulation. A previous negative antibody screen does not rule out the need to repeat it when hydrops is investigated. Tests are chosen and interpreted together, including when only one systemic effusion is present. Ask what each result would change, how soon it may return and who will explain it.

Genetic tests and different types of sampling

Current SMFM guidance recommends diagnostic genetic testing when one or more fetal effusions are detected, usually including chromosomal microarray with or without a karyotype. Selected infection tests may be performed on an appropriate sample. If these tests do not explain the findings, exome or genome sequencing may be offered, with genetic counselling; sometimes tests are considered together. Screening such as cell-free DNA cannot exclude all the genetic conditions that can cause hydrops, and a reassuring screening result is not a complete diagnostic answer.

Amniocentesis takes a sample of the fluid surrounding the fetus for selected tests. Fetal blood sampling, sometimes called cordocentesis or PUBS, takes fetal blood, often from the umbilical cord. These are different procedures. Both use ultrasound guidance; fetal blood sampling or transfusion is not guided by amniocentesis. Discuss the purpose, possible results, uncertainty, procedure risks and alternatives before deciding. Test availability, timing, costs and local services vary.

Treating selected cases of severe fetal anaemia

Severe fetal anaemia can sometimes be treated before birth with an intrauterine transfusion of appropriately matched donor red cells. This may be considered for immune disease and selected nonimmune causes, including some infections, inherited anaemias or fetal blood loss. The specialist may use fetal blood sampling to confirm the problem and give the transfusion during the same procedure when appropriate. This is specialist treatment, not a home intervention or a substitute for establishing the cause.

The choice between fetal treatment, continued monitoring and delivery depends on the cause, severity, pregnancy stage, maternal and fetal condition, available expertise and the family’s wishes. More than one transfusion may be needed, and treatment cannot guarantee survival or prevent every later problem. Ask about the expected benefit, procedure-related risks and the next review. Taking extra oral iron yourself does not replace assessment or treatment of fetal anaemia.

Other treatments and care when the cause is uncertain

Other selected causes require different approaches. Some fetal rhythm problems can be treated with medicines given to the pregnant person under specialist monitoring. A large chest fluid collection may be considered for needle drainage or a temporary shunt to reduce pressure. Particular structural, infectious or genetic conditions have their own management options. An intervention that is useful for one cause should not be assumed to help every baby with hydrops.

Not every case has an effective treatment during pregnancy, but an unexplained cause does not automatically mean that only comfort care is possible. The team can continue diagnostic work, reassess the course and plan maternal and newborn support. Discuss all appropriate options, including continuing pregnancy with monitoring or selected treatment, palliative care when relevant, and ending the pregnancy where available within local law and services. Emerging fetal therapies offered in research trials are not the same as established treatment.

The pregnant person also needs monitoring

Hydrops can be associated with serious maternal illness, including mirror syndrome, a pre-eclampsia-like condition in which maternal illness may accompany fetal fluid accumulation. It can affect blood pressure, breathing, kidney or liver function and blood tests. It does not always produce the complete combination of visible swelling, high blood pressure and protein in the urine. Do not wait to recognize every feature before asking for help.

The maternity team may arrange repeated blood-pressure checks, symptom reviews and laboratory tests. Get immediate maternity assessment for a severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, feeling very unwell, heartburn that does not settle with medicine, or vomiting. New breathlessness or noticeably reduced urine also needs immediate clinical assessment. Mirror syndrome can make continuing pregnancy dangerous; delivery or other pregnancy-management options require urgent individualized counselling rather than routine watchful waiting.

Discuss prognosis without treating a percentage as a prediction

Hydrops can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth or serious newborn illness. Chest fluid or swelling can limit lung growth or interfere with breathing and circulation. The underlying disease may bring additional risks. Outcomes vary with the cause, associated findings, timing, severity, response to treatment and the care the baby needs after birth. Earlier detection can be concerning, but pregnancy week alone does not determine the outcome.

Published studies include different diagnoses and populations, and some count only babies who were born alive. A general mortality estimate cannot accurately describe every pregnancy with nonimmune hydrops. Ask the fetal-medicine and neonatal teams what is known about this particular situation, what remains uncertain and which decisions may change as results return. Counselling should respect your priorities and include emotional support, without promising either a cure or an inevitable poor outcome.

Plan the timing, place and mode of birth

Birth planning involves maternal-fetal medicine, obstetric and neonatal specialists and, when needed, other teams. If immediate intensive treatment is anticipated or the cause remains uncertain, birth at a hospital able to stabilize and treat a critically ill newborn may be needed. Transfer of maternity care before birth may be safer than an unplanned newborn transfer. The plan should record the agreed neonatal resuscitation and treatment goals, including palliative care when chosen.

Hydrops does not automatically require caesarean birth or delivery at a fixed week. The team balances the risks of prematurity against maternal illness, labour or membrane rupture, worsening fetal findings and the risks of continuing pregnancy. Caesarean birth is used for appropriate obstetric indications. If preterm birth is expected and neonatal treatment is planned, ask whether antenatal corticosteroids or other preparation is appropriate. Decisions should be revisited when the condition or the family’s goals change.

What may happen in the newborn unit

A baby with persistent or severe hydrops may be very unwell at birth and need neonatal intensive care. Initial care can include breathing support, sometimes intubation and ventilation, treatment to support circulation, and intravenous medicines or nutrition. Selected fluid collections may need drainage if they impair breathing or circulation. Not every baby needs every procedure, and the care plan should explain why each intervention is being considered.

The neonatal team continues the search for the cause and checks how the baby responds. Some babies need surgery or another cause-specific treatment; others need time and supportive care. The degree of swelling alone does not determine the whole treatment plan. Ask who will update you, how you can be involved safely and what the next decision points are. Parents should not manipulate drains, shunts, lines or respiratory equipment themselves.

Anaemia, jaundice and glucose after birth

If red-cell antibodies caused the illness, the baby may need monitoring and treatment for anaemia or jaundice, including phototherapy or transfusion in selected circumstances. Anaemia can recur in the weeks after birth, including after a fetal transfusion, so follow-up matters even when the baby initially seems better. Ask about planned blood tests and whom to contact for paler colour, unusual sleepiness, poorer feeding or faster breathing.

Premature or unwell newborns may also need blood-glucose monitoring and treatment. Severe, persistent or recurrent low glucose can be harmful, but it is not correct to say that every baby with hydrops develops low glucose, seizures or brain injury. Signs such as poor feeding, altered alertness, jitteriness or abnormal movements can have several causes and require clinical assessment and appropriate measurement. Do not try to diagnose or treat them with a home feeding or sugar remedy.

Follow-up and support for the family

Recovery, feeding support, discharge and longer-term follow-up depend on the underlying condition, prematurity, treatment and the baby’s progress. Some children need ongoing heart, blood, genetic, developmental or other specialist care. Ask for written follow-up and medicine instructions, including any later anaemia testing. There is no standard hospital-stay length or promise that all problems end once the fluid improves.

A cause-specific diagnosis can also help explain whether a later pregnancy might be affected and whether testing or early monitoring would be useful. An unexplained result does not mean that every future pregnancy will have the same problem. Genetic counselling, social work, psychological support and palliative-care support can help families with uncertainty and difficult decisions. Needing help or choosing among medically appropriate options is not a failure of parenting.

When the pregnant person needs urgent help

Contact maternity care immediately for reduced, absent or changed usual fetal movements; do not wait for the next scan or use a home Doppler as reassurance. After amniocentesis or a fetal procedure, follow the centre’s written plan and seek urgent advice for vaginal fluid leakage or bleeding, fever or feeling hot/cold/shivery, contractions, or abdominal pain that does not settle or is worsening. Report the maternal warning symptoms described above immediately, even after birth, rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Use local emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to an arm, back, neck or jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion or a first seizure. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain needs emergency assessment; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion also does. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is another emergency pathway. These are alternative triggers, not signs that must all occur. The affected person must not drive to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

When a baby needs urgent help

If the baby is in hospital, alert staff immediately about a change in breathing, colour, feeding, alertness or movements. Outside hospital, seek immediate emergency assessment for difficulty breathing or very fast breathing; blue, grey, unusually pale or blotchy colour; cold or damp/clammy skin; difficulty waking or loss of consciousness; a seizure; a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; no urine for 12 hours; or a temperature of 38°C or more in a baby under 3 months, or below 36°C, or shivering. A baby who is not feeding, is not responding normally or is unusually sleepy also needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for all the signs or for a planned blood test.

Jaundice within the first 24 hours needs emergency assessment. In a baby, jaundice with unusual sleepiness or difficult waking, not feeding, floppiness or stiffness, jerking, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, feeling abnormally hot/cold or shivering, no wet nappies, or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice even without these emergency signs. Follow the baby’s individual discharge plan too. For emergency transport, ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask which fluid spaces are involved, what causes are being considered and what each blood, ultrasound, infection or genetic test can answer. Keep the test and result-review plan, and ask about counselling if results are uncertain.

Discuss the expected benefits, risks and alternatives of any fetal treatment and how maternal health changes the plan. Confirm the next assessment and urgent contact route rather than waiting for a routine scan when symptoms change.

Before birth or discharge, agree the place of care, newborn treatment goals, medicine and blood-test follow-up, and how you can participate safely. Ask for practical and emotional support; do not manipulate medical equipment or delay urgent assessment while keeping records.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointments, a symptom timeline, the written care plan and questions for fetal-medicine, maternity and neonatal teams. It cannot interpret scans or genetic results, determine the cause, select a procedure, predict survival, monitor a baby’s condition or replace urgent care. Do not delay contacting the team to finish a record.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care immediately for reduced or changed usual fetal movements; postprocedure bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or feeling hot/cold/shivery, contractions or unrelieved/worsening abdominal pain; or severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden face/hand/foot swelling, feeling very unwell, unrelieved heartburn, vomiting, new breathlessness or reduced urine. Use emergency services for severe breathing trouble, a tight/heavy chest, pain spreading to an arm/back/neck/jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion or a first seizure. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness/dizziness or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion, also needs emergency help. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness/dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is another emergency. The affected person must not drive; arrange another driver or an ambulance. A baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey/unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking, a seizure, a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry, no urine for 12 hours, not feeding or an abnormal response/unusual sleepiness needs emergency assessment. So does a temperature of 38°C or more under 3 months, below 36°C, or shivering. Jaundice before 24 hours, or jaundice with unusual sleepiness/difficult waking, not feeding, floppy/stiff/jerking movements, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, feeling abnormally hot/cold or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new/worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice. These are alternative triggers; do not wait for all of them. Ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Hydrops is a serious fluid-accumulation pattern with different causes; excess amniotic fluid or a large placenta is an associated finding, not a defining fetal compartment.
  • Immune red-cell disease and nonimmune causes need assessment. Anti-D prevention does not treat established antibodies or every cause of hydrops.
  • A single systemic effusion can merit a similar diagnostic work-up. Amniocentesis and fetal blood sampling are different procedures.
  • Selected causes may benefit from fetal treatment, but maternal safety, prognosis, pregnancy choices and birth plans require individualized counselling.
  • Newborn intensive care and later follow-up depend on the cause and response. Maternal illness or a baby’s emergency warning signs must not wait for the next appointment.

Frequently asked questions

What are the signs of fetal hydrops?

Ultrasound may show abnormal fluid in the abdomen, around the lungs or heart, or generalized swelling under the skin. Classical hydrops involves at least two fetal compartments. Excess amniotic fluid and a thickened placenta may accompany it but are not themselves defining compartments. One abnormal fluid collection can still warrant a comprehensive assessment; it should not automatically be dismissed as harmless.

How is fetal hydrops diagnosed and investigated?

Ultrasound identifies the fluid pattern, followed by a specialist assessment of anatomy, growth, heart structure/function, blood flow and possible causes. Maternal antibody and selected infection or blood tests help distinguish mechanisms. Diagnostic genetic testing is recommended when one or more fetal effusions are detected, with further sequencing considered if initial testing is unexplained. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid; fetal blood sampling samples fetal blood. A screening test or one normal result does not exclude every cause.

Can fetal hydrops be treated?

Sometimes a specific cause can be treated, for example with an intrauterine transfusion for selected severe fetal anaemia, medicine for certain fetal arrhythmias, or drainage for a significant chest effusion. Treatment choice and risk depend on the diagnosis, severity, pregnancy stage and available expertise. Not every case has an effective prenatal treatment, but an unknown cause does not automatically mean only palliative care. Discuss diagnostic, supportive, treatment and pregnancy-management options without expecting a guaranteed result.

What complications can occur?

Hydrops can be associated with pregnancy loss, preterm birth, impaired lung growth, breathing or circulatory problems and serious newborn illness. The underlying disorder may add other complications. Maternal mirror syndrome is also a serious risk. Premature or unwell babies may need glucose monitoring, but low glucose, seizures or brain injury are not inevitable consequences of hydrops. Individual counselling is more useful than a universal mortality percentage.

Does an anti-D injection prevent or treat all hydrops?

No. It helps prevent formation of immune anti-D in eligible circumstances. It does not remove established antibodies, prevent other clinically important red-cell antibodies such as anti-c or anti-K, or treat nonimmune causes. Blood-group differences alone do not show whether a fetus is affected. Follow the team’s antibody-testing, prevention and specialist assessment plan.

Is a fetal transfusion the same as amniocentesis?

No. Amniocentesis collects amniotic fluid for selected diagnostic tests. Fetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion involve the fetal circulation and may be considered for significant fetal anaemia. They use ultrasound guidance, not amniocentesis guidance. The specialist explains whether treatment, monitoring or delivery is appropriate, including risks and alternatives; taking extra oral iron is not a substitute.

Will the baby need a caesarean and intensive care?

There is no automatic caesarean or fixed delivery week for every case. Maternal health, fetal condition, gestation, appropriate obstetric indications and agreed treatment goals guide the plan. Persistent or severe hydrops may need birth at a centre with neonatal intensive care for breathing, circulation, drainage or cause-specific treatment. The team should discuss likely care before birth while explaining what remains uncertain.

Which changes mean we should get help immediately?

Contact maternity care immediately for reduced or changed usual fetal movements; postprocedure bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or feeling hot/cold/shivery, contractions or unrelieved/worsening abdominal pain; or severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden face/hand/foot swelling, feeling very unwell, unrelieved heartburn, vomiting, new breathlessness or reduced urine. Use emergency services for severe breathing trouble, a tight/heavy chest, pain spreading to an arm/back/neck/jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion or a first seizure. Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness/dizziness or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion, also needs emergency help. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness/dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is another emergency. The affected person must not drive; arrange another driver or an ambulance. A baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey/unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking, a seizure, a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry, no urine for 12 hours, not feeding or an abnormal response/unusual sleepiness needs emergency assessment. So does a temperature of 38°C or more under 3 months, below 36°C, or shivering. Jaundice before 24 hours, or jaundice with unusual sleepiness/difficult waking, not feeding, floppy/stiff/jerking movements, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, feeling abnormally hot/cold or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new/worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice. These are alternative triggers; do not wait for all of them. Ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
